title: Fractals through the hands
subtitle: A proposed overhaul of seven existing halls: one rule, many consequences of scale.
status: Proposal after source review. Museum code, order, tutorial.md and final.md unchanged.
thesis: Forces asks what follows a push. Fractals can ask what follows another application of the same rule. The surprise can be perfectly deterministic: more pieces, less material; a longer boundary between unchanged endpoints; an opening that exists but cannot admit us.
recommendation: Keep the seven-hall order. Develop one primary interaction for each principle, complete its runnable tutorial, then curate the surrounding collection. Begin with a hand-controlled recursive canopy, while repairing the short Recursion prerequisite lesson first.

halls.title: Again — until what?
halls.alt: Shrinking coloured doorway frames stand beside the existing square-recursion desk inside the museum.
halls.existing: The square desk and matching shrinking doorways already connect a repeated scale operation with the visitor's body. MORE, LESS and layout controls expose finite terms. Keep this encounter.
halls.proposal: Add a nearby held handle that unfolds one generation at a time. A separate, clearly marked scale handle changes the reduction factor. Highlight the current call, parent and stopping condition. Keep a stable bypass beside the doorway sequence.
halls.lesson: Return to the line/frame construction the student already knows. Make one frame, call the same construction with a smaller size and one fewer remaining step, then stop. Show the complete small script and its supplied dependencies. The first independent change is the reduction factor; the student predicts the next size before running it. Factorial, memoisation, tail recursion and pixel mapping move out of this first lesson.
halls.reflection: The instruction can continue after an opening has become useless to this body. Computational continuation, visibility and passage have different limits.
halls.check: Depth zero emits nothing; three requested terms produce three frames when above the minimum size; adjacent sizes follow the declared factor. Boundary inputs terminate without removing the room's bypass.
halls.carry: A bounded generating function and an explicit record of the terms it produced.

halls.title: One gesture, many descendants
halls.alt: The museum canopy branches overhead, with smaller trees visible beside it.
halls.existing: A large canopy already follows the growth study. The primary tree grows from queued branch records; its console changes angle, length and fork count. A second tree supports inspection of its existing structure.
halls.proposal: Put two familiar point grips on a small parent-and-children model. Moving a grip changes a child direction; descendants inherit the local rule and the room-sized canopy previews it. Offer one-generation growth beside the hand. Begin with fixed deterministic geometry; use a held seed when later comparing irregular growth.
halls.lesson: Extend the known line into two shorter children at its endpoint. Store start, direction, length and depth as a branch record. Reuse the previous stopping condition, then show how a queue lets the museum reveal a generation without pretending this source is a direct self-call. Compare two and three children only after the two-child construction works. Save a chosen rule and seed for later reconstruction.
halls.reflection: A small choice near the root can become the shape of the whole canopy. Repetition distributes an earlier decision; it does not make that decision inevitable.
halls.check: Every child begins at its parent's endpoint. A complete binary tree through depth four has 31 segments including the trunk. Altering the selected subtree leaves its sibling unchanged; replaying the same seed and rule reproduces the geometry.
halls.carry: A branch recipe, with a named root, local coordinates and optional fixed seed.

halls.title: Make room by removing
halls.anchor: cantor_set; pagoda as the body-scale comparison
halls.alt: A narrow opening between pink Cantor-pagoda pillars frames the museum beyond.
halls.existing: The interval study already separates latest state, history and ghost removals. The pagoda turns repeated removal into gaps of different widths. Preserve those distinctions.
halls.proposal: Let the player pull a removable middle-third handle, then apply that same cut to the current generation. Show only the newest rule application first; history stays optional. Bring the held sphere to the pagoda as a probe before trying the player's own body.
halls.lesson: Reuse arrays and the current/next pattern encountered earlier in the spine. Replace each interval by its two outer thirds, keeping the source row intact. Count the survivors and sum their lengths. The learner changes one legal retained fraction in a clearly labelled variant, while the canonical thirds remain available for comparison. Save the generated intervals for the final hall.
halls.reflection: More pieces can occupy less material. A hole can admit a point, a sphere or a person differently; counting holes does not establish access.
halls.check: For the standard thirds rule, generation n has 2^n intervals and total length L(2/3)^n. Hiding history changes neither result. Ghost middles stay non-solid and the original record remains intact.
halls.carry: Ordered intervals, the rule that made them and a retained original record.

halls.title: The shortest way becomes longer
halls.anchor: fractal_koch_curve; Sierpinski and measurement as successive comparisons
halls.alt: An orange Koch curve holds fixed endpoints above its control desk, with a triangular construction behind it.
halls.existing: The Koch desk compares endpoint distance with path length. Sierpinski exposes kept and removed area. A separate box-counting instrument holds its sample while changing measurement scales. These are valuable but dense together.
halls.proposal: Move the familiar point along a widened, supported floor drawing of the Koch route; compare direct distance with distance travelled. A nearby control replaces each segment once. Then visit the cut triangle. Keep box counting in a quieter optional study bay with an unchanged sample.
halls.lesson: Reuse the line endpoints and segment list. One classical Koch step replaces one segment by four at one-third length; the next generation reads the previous list without editing it in place. Test this before adding the separate Sierpinski triangle operation. The held point reads the construction and its measurement; the tutorial does not rebuild locomotion or introduce springs here.
halls.reflection: The ends remain where they were while the route between them grows. A measurement depends on the path and on the scale at which we inspect it.
halls.check: For the standard 60-degree Koch rule, 4^n segments join without gaps, endpoints stay fixed and length is L(4/3)^n. At four steps a four-metre seed measures about 12.642 metres. Test a variant separately rather than borrowing the standard formula.
halls.carry: A reusable segment replacement and the distinction between endpoint distance and path length.

halls.title: The cube becomes a place
halls.alt: The view from a Menger-sponge passage shows nested openings in dark geometry edged in pink.
halls.existing: The nine-metre sponge, two finite cuts, retained solid cells and flight enclosure already exist. The desk refuses geometry changes while a visitor is inside. This is already a strong climax.
halls.proposal: Add a reachable miniature with a 3×3×3 cell-selection preview. Point to a removed cell and see its correspondence on the large cube. Apply only from outside an empty enclosure. Offer the familiar thrust-point interface through the existing flight ownership system, after testing entry, release and exit together.
halls.lesson: Return to the student's cube and grid addresses. Divide one cube into 27 cells and specify which seven are removed before repeating on the twenty survivors. Produce the small construction first. The museum supplies the large display and movement service; the lesson explains that boundary instead of concealing a whole player system in the example.
halls.reflection: Seeing through, having a connected route and being able to pass through are different achievements. Removing material can create a place while still excluding a body.
halls.check: At n cuts, standard Menger has 20^n retained cells and volume fraction (20/27)^n. Two cuts give 400 cells. Independently verify collision and real route clearance, refusal to rebuild around an occupant, and a working ground exit.
halls.carry: The same replacement reasoning applied to volume; an explicit distinction between generated data and bodily access.

halls.title: A number still needs a form
halls.alt: An upright golden rectangle is divided into coloured squares with measured side labels.
halls.existing: The numerical sequence already compares linear and logarithmic height mappings. The rectangle shows cuts, side lengths and circular arcs. Keep it as a quieter comparison after the sponge.
halls.proposal: Make the first two values tangible tiles; bring them together to request the next sum. Offer two adjacent, labelled mappings of the same held values. Let the player slide a square cut into the rectangle, keeping the measurements beside the hand.
halls.lesson: Reuse the known array to retain successive sums. Change how the same values determine visible size while preserving the values themselves. Then compare the separate geometric rule of the golden rectangle. This can be a short consolidation lesson: numerical recurrence is not automatically recursive geometry, and a proportion does not prove beauty.
halls.reflection: A relationship becomes a form through additional choices. Preserve the pleasure of the arrangement while making those choices available to question.
halls.check: The next value equals the previous two. Changing a height mapping leaves the numerical record unchanged. Rectangle measurements support the stated ratio; circular arc construction is labelled without claiming it is an exact logarithmic spiral.
halls.carry: A held record plus explicit mapping choices; a pause before the final composition.

halls.title: Choose what gets to repeat
halls.alt: The existing synthesis collection includes a dark sphere, branching structure and suspended cloud inside the museum.
halls.existing: The hall compares concrete procedures and already leads to the Cantor preset in the following L-system laboratory. The grammar F→FfF, f→fff is implemented. Julia, Mandelbrot and CrossSequence remain extensions outside this seven-hall route.
halls.proposal: Give the saved interval or branching recipe a physical card. Place it beside a simple seed; inspect the first step before expanding to room scale. Allow one parameter edit, freeze a chosen result and compare with the saved version. Show seed, replacement and stop together. Audit storage before promising a cross-hall import.
halls.lesson: Rebuild a previously saved construction from its declared recipe. The student changes one choice and predicts a difference. Reconstruct Cantor from the existing two-symbol grammar, with step size normalised to the same total span, and compare the intervals to the earlier saved record. The next sequence owns the general rewriting system; this hall demonstrates why one is useful.
halls.reflection: Which rule has been repeated, and who has room in the result? Complexity alone answers neither question. The selected work can remain particular rather than becoming a compulsory catalogue of every specimen.
halls.check: A saved recipe reconstructs its stated output within tolerance. Comparison does not mutate the original. At equal depth and normalised span, Cantor's symbols and interval construction agree. Every recipe declares and obeys a finite budget.
halls.carry: One authored construction and an exact question for L-systems: how can a written rule acquire a spatial reader?

optional_play.name: The hydra that grows when you attack
optional_play.idea: The project has a fractal_hydra with bounded head splitting. Audit its damage targeting and controller path before placing it. Killing-as-growth can make the stopping rule matter, but repeated branching alone should not be presented as a complete definition of a fractal.

optional_play.name: The Catalyst splits its answer
optional_play.idea: Fractal-mode projectiles already describe three children per split and a depth limit of two. Display ancestry and a generation counter. Verify configuration, lifetime and the count of living parents plus children before calling the weapon a working lesson.

optional_play.name: A chair that repeats itself out of use
optional_play.idea: Let one seating surface acquire smaller descendants until sitting, looking and carrying become different demands. Keep its actual selection algorithm explicit: the recursive_chair name alone is not evidence of a self-calling function.
